newsitem.title: NORWAY: Shipowners switch registers to avoid costs - DNV.
newsitem.headline: Shipowners switch registers to avoid costs - DNV.

text.p: International classification society Det Norske Veritas (DNV) said on Wednesday many shipowners were transferring old vessels to less rigorous registers in order to avoid costly upgrading work.

The Oslo-based society said it had deleted 233 ships from its register in 1996, including 80 because of overdue surveys or for not fulfilling recommendations. The remaining ships were transferred to other classification societies by owners.
The average age of vessels struck off from class was 17.8 years. The average age of vessels transferred to other major classification societies was 12 years, DNV said.
It said the figures showed that many old vessels were transferred to minor or national classification societies, which lack an international network of offices to uphold stringent requirements.
The oldest vessels -- 187 with an average age close to 19 years -- mainly went to others without membership to the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS).

"Many of the ships were deleted from our classes because the owners did not want to invest in the necessary upgrading," DNV said in a statement. "It is a problem that many of the minor classification societies will vouch for these ships without asking questions."
Instead of scrapping vessels, some owners speculated in keeping them afloat for a few more years.
"That is the worst...part of the shipping industry, which contributes to giving the whole sector a bad reputation," DNV said.
It said the five major classification societies -- DNV, American Bureau of Shipping, Lloyd's Register, Japan's NK and Germanische Lloyd's -- held between 80 and 90 percent of the world's fleet.
DNV has a fleet of 4,400 vessels with 278 offices in 100 countries.

"When an owner takes a ship at 19.5 years and switches from a major to a small national classification society with no network, that's an indication that there's something rotten here," said DNV spokesman Ole Kristian Lunde.
